05 - Summary: can genomic selection improve nitrogen use efficiency?

Holstein / Red Dairy Cattle / Jersey in Denmark, Sweden, Finland and Germany (simulation)

Prepared for Emmanuel Ismaila

2026-11-11

1 How to read this report

Everything below is read from files written by 00-04; nothing is typed in. It is a simulation: genetic parameters come from the literature (file 00), but the population, its genomes and its phenotypes are simulated, so results show what the design implies, not what real Nordic data would show. Units are genetic standard deviations of the founder population unless stated. GS_NTM, GS_NTM_NUE35, GS_NTM_NUE75, GS_NTM_NUE35_MUN, the methane scenario (GS_NTM_NUE75_CH4) and GS_NTM_NUE35_OCS_dF1 were run with up to 10 replicates, each from its own independent coalescent founder population and burn-in (7 Nov 2026, your choice); PHENO and GS_NTM_NUE35_MATE once (replicate 0). Within a replicate all scenarios share the founders, burn-in and random-number stream, so scenario differences are paired. Only the replicate section tests whether a difference between programmes is consistent; single-run differences in the earlier tables are indicative only. Genomic EBVs in file 04 came from SNPBLUP, the winner of the head-to-head test in 04b. Genomic-prediction accuracies come from one cross-validation run per dataset (3 folds + forward), so differences below about 0.05 are within fold-to-fold noise.

3 Breeding goal: NTM weights and the expected price of NUE (file 00)

The indices use the official NTM sub-index weights (May 2026) for the five sub-indices that have a simulated counterpart (Yield = milk + protein yield with Kargo et al. 2014 economic values, Fertility = ICF, Udder health = SCS, Longevity, Saved Feed = SF, the NAV Saved Feed trait since 7 Nov 2026). NTM has no weight for NUE, MUN or CH4; NUE is added at 0.35 (the Saved Feed weight) or 0.75, MUN at -0.35 on top of NUE 0.35, and CH4 on top of one NUE weight at the knee of the CH4 weight sweep (file 00; chosen: GS_NTM_NUE75_CH4, CH4 weight -0.5). Mapping and assumptions: file 00.

Genomic REML relative to the true within-breed h2 (ratio): SCS 0.00, CH4 0.37, LONG 0.55, LNVAR 0.56, ICF 0.62, MY 0.65, PY 0.71, SF 0.84, FY 0.88, MUN 0.92, NUE 1.12. A ratio below 1 is genetic variance the SNP panel (about 10k) does not capture (de los Campos et al. 2015). Pedigree REML was within 20% of the true value for MY, SF, LNVAR, MUN, FY and further off for PY (0.71), SCS (0.54), ICF (2.19), LONG (0.53), NUE (0.80), CH4 (0.67); with 3,000 records, low-h2 traits carry little information.

5 Genomic prediction: cross-validated accuracy (file 02)

Every model fits breed and herd x generation as fixed effects (file 02), so no model estimates the genetic differences between breeds, and file 04 selects within breed. The accuracy that matters is therefore the within-breed correlation between EBV and true breeding value (averaged over breeds, weighted by cows). The pooled correlation over all three breeds is shown second, because it also rewards or penalises arbitrary breed-level offsets in the EBVs.

traits_cv <- c("NUE", "MUN", "SF", "CH4")
cv <- rbindlist(lapply(traits_cv, function(t) rd(sprintf("cv_results_%s.csv", t))), fill = TRUE)
cv9 <- rd("cv_results_NUE.csv", params$gxe_dir)
if (!is.null(cv9)) cv <- rbind(cv, cv9[, trait := "NUE_rg0.9"], fill = TRUE)
cv <- cv[model != "GBLUP_snp"]
cvs <- cv[, .(acc_wb = mean(acc_within_breed), acc = mean(acc_TBV), slope = mean(slope)),
          by = .(trait, model, scheme = ifelse(scheme == "forward", "forward", "k-fold"))]
kable(dcast(cvs, model ~ trait + scheme, value.var = "acc_wb"), digits = 3,
      caption = "Within-breed accuracy = cor(EBV, true BV) within breed, n-weighted mean (the accuracy that matters for selection)")

Cross-examination of the working assumption that ssGBLUP gives good EBVs.

  • Breed-level offsets in single-step EBVs. In this run ssGBLUP’s pooled NUE accuracy in the youngest generation was 0.01 (slope 0.04) against a within-breed accuracy of 0.15, and its breed means were not in the order of the true breed means (JER ranked lowest). In the archived run with the 9-correlation matrix (1-3 Nov), the same model gave a pooled accuracy of 0.00 against 0.24 within breed, because it ranked the breed with the highest true mean lowest. So the breed-level part of single-step EBVs is unstable between runs. Because breed is a fixed effect, that part carries no information in any model, and it is consistent with the known incompatibility between the genomic matrix G and the pedigree matrix A22 (different bases and genetic means) in single-step evaluation (Vitezica et al. 2011, Genet Res 93:357-366). Correction (7 Nov 2026): an earlier version said that no adjustment was tested. In fact ssGBLUP has always used G rescaled to A22 (a + bG, Christensen et al. 2012), pooled over the three breeds. Since 7 Nov the breed-metafounder model (ssGBLUP_MF; Legarra et al. 2015, Genetics 200:455-468) is fitted alongside it; the comparison is below.
  • Pooled-adjusted G vs metafounders. Chosen per trait (decision rule of file 02: within-breed accuracy, ties within 1 SE broken by dispersion slope): NUE ssGBLUP (MF minus pooled -0.001, SE 0.000); MUN ssGBLUP_MF (MF minus pooled +0.000, SE 0.000); SF ssGBLUP_MF (MF minus pooled +0.000, SE 0.000); CH4 ssGBLUP_MF (MF minus pooled -0.000, SE 0.000). Mean gap between G and A22 relationships across breed blocks: pooled-adjusted 0.079, metafounder 0.006 (absolute mean over blocks; file 02). Why this matters: with pooled rescaling the between-breed blocks of G and A22 cannot all match at once, so EBVs carry an arbitrary breed offset; metafounders give each breed its own base, so G05 and AΓ22 agree by construction. Within-breed ranking, which is what file 04 uses, is affected only through the within-breed blocks.
  • Within breed, the best model was: NUE ssGBLUP (0.29) k-fold and ssGBLUP (0.15) forward; MUN ssGBLUP_MF (0.34) and ssGBLUP_MF (0.28); Saved Feed ssGBLUP_MF (0.30) and ssGBLUP_MF (0.24); CH4 ssGBLUP (0.26) and ssGBLUP (0.21). With between-country r_g 0.9: NUE ABLUP (0.25) k-fold and ABLUP (0.27) forward. Differences below about 0.05 are within fold-to-fold noise (one run per dataset).
  • GBLUP and rrBLUP agree exactly, as theory requires. BayesA/B do not improve on GBLUP under this polygenic architecture.
  • Weighted ssGBLUP is not recommended: after the SNP-weight iteration REML fitted h2 of 0.45 to 0.91 (true values are far lower), and its EBVs are strongly over-dispersed.
  • Real-data benchmark. For Finnish Red cows, Chegini et al. (2026, Front Genet 17:1815864) report ssGBLUP forward-validation correlations of 0.33-0.53 and dispersion 0.45-0.75 for feed-efficiency traits. Their correlations are computed against real (corrected) phenotypes, so they are not the same quantity as accuracy against true breeding values here and cannot be ranked against it. Their dispersion range does show that over-dispersion of this size also occurs in real single-step evaluations.

Multi-trait reading. Two separate questions:

  • Prediction: when NUE and MUN are unrecorded on young cows but their other traits are recorded (N_masked), NUE accuracy was UN 0.09, DIAG 0.01, FA -0.04; the most accurate model was UN, and DIC was lowest for UN. Only models whose accuracy exceeds DIAG (no genetic covariances) gain from the correlations.
  • Parameter estimation: with 1,500 cows and 11 traits, posterior heritabilities are pulled towards the prior (compressed range: 0.14 to 0.68 against true values of 0.04 to 0.42) and genetic correlations are shrunk towards zero (slope of estimated on realised rg: UN 0.35, FA 0.17), though their pattern is recovered (correlation between estimated and realised r_g: UN 0.63, FA 0.56). These Bayesian (co)variances should not be used as parameter estimates at this data size; the single-trait REML values in Section 3 are more reliable.

GxE reading. REML likelihood-ratio tests of the compound-symmetry model against no GxE: on the control data (no GxE simulated) MY p = 0.089 (converged); NUE p = 0.078 (converged); on the data simulated with rg = 0.9 MY p = 0.018 (converged); NUE p = 0.126 (converged). Standard errors of the between-country rg were 0.40 to 1.29. The Bayesian verdict (both priors must agree) was - control: MY: no important GxE; NUE: uninformative (prior-dependent); GxE data: MY: uninformative (prior-dependent); NUE: uninformative (prior-dependent). Estimating GxE of this size needs far more genotyped and recorded cows per country than the 1,500-cow subsample used here. The GxE dataset came from a separate coalescent run, so its accuracies are not a paired comparison with the control dataset.

8 Replicates: how robust are the scenario differences?

The six main scenarios were each run on up to 10 replicates. Each replicate has its own coalescent founder population and burn-in (file 01 with rep_id r: seed + r, which also changes the MaCS seed), so the spread between replicates now includes founder sampling, Mendelian sampling, phenotypes, training samples and matings. The same founders and seed are used for every scenario within a replicate, so differences are paired.

NTM value of a response. For each breed, the genetic change in each trait is divided by its standardisation SD (file 04, gs_sdA0.csv), multiplied by that breed’s GS_NTM weight and by 10 (NTM index units per SD), and summed: the change in the simulated part of NTM. Multiplied by EUR per NTM unit (HOL 9.9, RDC 9.2, JER 8.0 per cow-year; Fikse & Kargo 2020) it is the extra income per cow-year of daughters at the end, excluding non-simulated sub-indices.

rep_sc <- c("GS_NTM", "GS_NTM_NUE35", "GS_NTM_NUE75", "GS_NTM_NUE35_MUN", ch4_sc, "GS_NTM_NUE35_OCS_dF1")
R <- 0:(params$n_rep - 1)
read_rep <- function(kind, s, r, dir = rep_dir(r))
  rd(sprintf("gs_%s_%s%s.csv", kind, s, if (r == 0) "" else paste0("_rep", r)), dir)
w_ntm <- iw[index == "GS_NTM"]
# response = final generation minus the last burn-in generation OF THE SAME REPLICATE
resp_of <- function(s, r, dir = rep_dir(r)) {
  tr <- read_rep("trend", s, r, dir); tb <- rd("trend_burnin.csv", dir); if (is.null(tr) || is.null(tb)) return(NULL)
  merge(tr[generation == max(generation), .(breed, trait, end = mean_G)],
        tb[generation == max(generation), .(breed, trait, start = mean_G)], by = c("breed", "trait"))[, response := end - start][]
}
reps <- rbindlist(lapply(rep_sc, function(s) rbindlist(lapply(R, function(r) {
  resp <- resp_of(s, r); Fd <- read_rep("inbreeding", s, r); sdA0 <- rd("gs_sdA0.csv", rep_dir(r))
  if (is.null(resp) || is.null(Fd) || is.null(sdA0)) return(NULL)
  v <- merge(merge(resp, sdA0, by = "trait"), w_ntm[, .(breed, trait, w = weight)], by = c("breed", "trait"))
  ntm <- v[, .(NTM = 10 * sum(w * response / sdA0)), by = breed][, EUR := NTM * eur_per_ntm[breed]]
  dF <- Fd[, .(dF = 1 - ((1 - F_genomic[generation == max(generation)]) /
                           (1 - F_genomic[generation == min(generation)]))^(1 / (max(generation) - min(generation)))),
           by = breed]
  out <- dcast(resp[trait %in% c("NUE", "MUN", "CH4", "MY", "PY", "SF", "SCS", "ICF", "LONG")], breed ~ trait, value.var = "response")
  Reduce(function(a, b) merge(a, b, by = "breed"), list(out, ntm, dF))[, `:=`(scenario = s, replicate = r)]
}))))
if (nrow(reps)) {
  # tidy copies for the spreadsheet (NUE_replicate_results.xlsx)
  rep_long <- rbindlist(lapply(rep_sc, function(s) rbindlist(lapply(R, function(r) {
    x <- resp_of(s, r); if (is.null(x)) return(NULL)
    x[trait %in% c("NUE", "MUN", "CH4", "MY", "PY", "SF")][, `:=`(scenario = s, replicate = r,
      source = sprintf("%s/gs_trend_%s%s.csv", rep_dir(r), s, if (r == 0) "" else paste0("_rep", r)))]
  }))))
  fwrite(rep_long, file.path(params$base_dir, "replicate_response_long.csv"))
  fwrite(reps[, .(scenario, replicate, breed, dF, NTM, EUR,
                  source = sprintf("%s/gs_inbreeding_%s%s.csv", sapply(replicate, rep_dir), scenario, ifelse(replicate == 0, "", paste0("_rep", replicate))))],
         file.path(params$base_dir, "replicate_dF.csv"))
  pk(reps[, .(n = uniqueN(replicate)), by = scenario], caption = "Replicates available per scenario")
  long <- melt(reps, id.vars = c("scenario", "replicate", "breed"))
  pk(dcast(long[, .(txt = if (.BY$variable == "dF") sprintf("%.4f +/- %.4f", mean(value), sd(value)) else sprintf("%.2f +/- %.2f", mean(value), sd(value))), by = .(scenario, breed, variable)],
              breed + variable ~ scenario, value.var = "txt"),
        caption = "Response over 10 selection generations (genetic SD; NTM = index units; EUR = per cow-year) and rate of inbreeding (dF): mean +/- SD over replicates")
  pair_test <- function(a, b, v) {
    w <- merge(reps[scenario == a, c("replicate", "breed", v), with = FALSE],
               reps[scenario == b, c("replicate", "breed", v), with = FALSE], by = c("replicate", "breed"))
    if (nrow(w) == 0) return(NULL)
    w[, d := get(paste0(v, ".x")) - get(paste0(v, ".y"))]
    w[, .(n = .N, mean_diff = mean(d), sd_diff = sd(d), same_sign = max(sum(d > 0), sum(d < 0)),
          p_paired = if (.N > 1 && sd(d) > 0) t.test(d)$p.value else NA_real_), by = breed][, comparison := paste(a, "-", b)][, trait := v][]
  }
  pt <- rbindlist(lapply(c("NUE", "MUN", "CH4", "MY", "PY", "SF", "NTM", "EUR", "dF"), function(v) rbind(
    pair_test("GS_NTM_NUE35", "GS_NTM", v), pair_test("GS_NTM_NUE75", "GS_NTM", v),
    pair_test("GS_NTM_NUE35_MUN", "GS_NTM_NUE35", v), pair_test(ch4_sc, ch4_base, v),
    pair_test("GS_NTM_NUE35_OCS_dF1", "GS_NTM_NUE35", v))))
  pk(pt[, .(comparison, trait, breed, n, mean_diff, sd_diff, same_sign, p_paired)], digits = 4,
        caption = "Paired differences between scenarios (same seed within replicate); same_sign = replicates with the majority sign; paired t-test")
}

With n replicates the paired t-test has n - 1 degrees of freedom; p-values are per breed and per comparison without correction for multiple testing, so treat them as a guide to consistency across founder populations, not as a formal claim about real populations.

Simulation vs selection-index theory. The ratio of NUE responses (NUE index / NTM index) from the simulation is compared with the ratio expected from file 00 (true breeding values, infinite population). Agreement checks that the simulated programme behaves as the index design intends; differences come from EBV accuracy, finite population and changing variances.

if (nrow(reps)) {
  sim_ratio <- reps[, .(NUE = mean(NUE), NTM = mean(NTM)), by = .(scenario, breed)]
  sim_ratio <- merge(sim_ratio[scenario %in% c("GS_NTM_NUE35", "GS_NTM_NUE75")],
                     sim_ratio[scenario == "GS_NTM", .(breed, NUE0 = NUE, NTM0 = NTM)], by = "breed")
  sim_ratio[, nue_weight := ifelse(scenario == "GS_NTM_NUE35", 0.35, 0.75)]
  th <- merge(fr[nue_weight %in% c(0.35, 0.75), .(breed, nue_weight, NUE_th = NUE, NTM_th = NTM_pct_of_max / 100)],
              fr[nue_weight == 0, .(breed, NUE0_th = NUE)], by = "breed")
  cmp_th <- merge(sim_ratio, th, by = c("breed", "nue_weight"))
  kable(cmp_th[, .(breed, scenario, NUE_ratio_sim = NUE / NUE0, NUE_ratio_theory = NUE_th / NUE0_th,
                   NTM_ratio_sim = NTM / NTM0, NTM_ratio_theory = NTM_th)], digits = 3,
        caption = "NUE and NTM response relative to GS_NTM: simulation (replicate means) vs selection-index theory")
}

9 Sensitivity: how much do the conclusions rest on the NUE correlations?

Every NUE correlation was multiplied by s = 0 and s = 0.5 (file 00; s = 1 is the main run), and new founders, burn-ins and the GS_NTM and GS_NTM_NUE35 programmes were run for each level (up to 5 replicates per level). s = 0 means NUE is genetically unrelated to every other trait. A third set uses the heritability of the NAV Saved Feed index itself, 0.08 (Lidauer et al., NAV workshop 2026), instead of 0.23 (ReFI) (your choice, 7 Nov 2026).

sens_dir <- function(set, r) paste0(params$base_dir, if (set == "main") "" else paste0("_", set), if (r == 0) "" else paste0("_rep", r))
sens <- rbindlist(lapply(c("NUEx0", "NUEx05", "SFh008", "main"), function(set) rbindlist(lapply(0:(params$n_sens_rep - 1), function(r)
  rbindlist(lapply(c("GS_NTM", "GS_NTM_NUE35"), function(s) {
    x <- resp_of(s, r, sens_dir(set, r)); sd0 <- rd("gs_sdA0.csv", sens_dir(set, r))
    if (is.null(x) || is.null(sd0)) return(NULL)
    v <- merge(merge(x, sd0, by = "trait"), w_ntm[, .(breed, trait, w = weight)], by = c("breed", "trait"))
    merge(merge(x[trait == "NUE", .(breed, NUE = response)], x[trait == "SF", .(breed, SF = response)], by = "breed"),
          v[, .(NTM = 10 * sum(w * response / sdA0)), by = breed], by = "breed")[
      , `:=`(set = set, replicate = r, scenario = s)]
  }))))), fill = TRUE)
if (nrow(sens)) {
  sens[, set_label := c(NUEx0 = "NUE correlations x 0", NUEx05 = "NUE correlations x 0.5",
                        SFh008 = "Saved Feed h2 0.08", main = "main run")[set]]
  sw2 <- dcast(sens, set_label + breed + replicate ~ scenario, value.var = c("NUE", "SF", "NTM"))
  sw2[, `:=`(dNUE = NUE_GS_NTM_NUE35 - NUE_GS_NTM, dNTM = NTM_GS_NTM_NUE35 - NTM_GS_NTM)]
  sens_tab <- sw2[, .(n = .N, NUE_under_NTM = mean(NUE_GS_NTM), SF_under_NTM = mean(SF_GS_NTM),
                      NUE_gain_from_weight = mean(dNUE),
                      p_NUE = if (.N > 1 && sd(dNUE) > 0) t.test(dNUE)$p.value else NA_real_,
                      NTM_change = mean(dNTM)), by = .(set_label, breed)][order(breed, set_label)]
  pk(sens_tab, digits = 3, caption = "Sensitivity sets: NUE and Saved Feed response under NTM alone, extra NUE from the 0.35 weight, and NTM change (paired within replicate)")
  th_s <- fread("params/nue_sensitivity_theory.csv")
  pk(th_s, digits = 3, caption = "The same comparison from selection-index theory (file 00)")
}

Reading. If the NUE gain under NTM alone falls towards 0 as s goes to 0, NTM improves NUE only through the correlations, and the claim “NTM already improves NUE” depends on the Irish estimates. If the extra gain from the NUE weight stays clearly positive at every s, the recommendation to add an NUE weight does not depend on them.

10 Recommended breeding plan

Every number in this section is computed from the replicate table above (10 paired replicates, mean difference and paired t-test p per breed), or read from files 00-03. The parameters it rests on are listed in file 00 and the README.

  1. Evaluation model. Cross-validation (file 02): a single-step model (pooled-adjusted or metafounder) was the best model or within 0.05 of the best in 10 of 10 trait x validation-scheme comparisons. Inside the breeding programme (04b, 2 replicates of GS_NTM_NUE35): SNPBLUP: NTM +5.91, NUE +3.82, 37 s per evaluation (x1.0); ssGBLUP: could not be run (killed for exceeding the ~6.1 GB memory limit of the local machine, 8 Nov 2026), so SNPBLUP was used for all replicate runs (rule: ssGBLUP only if higher NTM and not lower NUE response at no more than twice the run time). For routine evaluation the single-step family remains the standard because it uses cows that have CFIT records but no genotypes; within it, the compatibility method chosen in file 02 is listed in the cross-validation section. Weighted ssGBLUP should not be used (over-dispersed EBVs).
  2. Selection index: NTM already improves NUE. An added NUE weight raised NUE further (significant in 3 of 3 breeds at 0.75, 3 of 3 at 0.35); its cost in NTM was significant in 2 breed x weight comparisons. Over 10 generations, in genetic SD (NTM and EUR: genetic level after 10 generations, EUR per cow-year):
    • Under NTM alone (GS_NTM), NUE rose by HOL 3.40, JER 3.40, RDC 3.32, carried by protein yield (rg PY-NUE 0.80, Tavernier et al. 2024).
    • Adding NUE at 0.35 (GS_NTM_NUE35 - GS_NTM): NUE HOL +1.08 (p < 0.001), JER +0.94 (p = 0.001), RDC +0.82 (p = 0.003); NTM value HOL +4.7 (p = 0.038), JER +0.5 (p = 0.793), RDC +2.0 (p = 0.261) index units, i.e. HOL +46.4 (p = 0.038), JER +4.0 (p = 0.793), RDC +18.6 (p = 0.261) EUR per cow-year.
    • Adding NUE at 0.75 (GS_NTM_NUE75 - GS_NTM): NUE HOL +1.43 (p < 0.001), JER +0.95 (p = 0.002), RDC +1.20 (p < 0.001); NTM value HOL -0.2 (p = 0.846), JER -2.9 (p = 0.041), RDC +0.8 (p = 0.614) index units, i.e. HOL -1.8 (p = 0.846), JER -22.9 (p = 0.041), RDC +7.5 (p = 0.614) EUR per cow-year.
    • Correlated changes at weight 0.35: CH4 HOL +0.60 (p = 0.003), JER +0.35 (p = 0.033), RDC +0.01 (p = 0.941); MUN HOL -0.13 (p = 0.350), JER -0.01 (p = 0.971), RDC +0.06 (p = 0.672); milk yield HOL +0.63 (p = 0.004), JER +0.07 (p = 0.696), RDC +0.44 (p = 0.004). Because the two indices differ only in the NUE weight, these are effects of that weight.
    • Correlated changes at weight 0.75: CH4 HOL +0.24 (p = 0.083), JER +0.05 (p = 0.773), RDC -0.08 (p = 0.621); protein yield HOL +0.51 (p < 0.001), JER +0.14 (p = 0.419), RDC +0.44 (p = 0.007); Saved Feed HOL -0.35 (p = 0.130), JER -0.50 (p = 0.020), RDC -0.07 (p = 0.592).
    • Under NTM alone, methane concentration rose (HOL 1.89, JER 1.60, RDC 2.10), through its sourced positive correlations with yield (Schneider et al. 2025). NTM has no methane weight.
    • Why the NTM cost is not seen. Selection-index theory (file 00) puts the NTM loss after 10 generations at about HOL 1.6, JER 1.6, RDC 1.3 index units at weight 0.35 and HOL 4.8, JER 5.0, RDC 4.1 at 0.75. The replicate-to-replicate SD of the paired NTM difference was HOL 6.1, JER 5.9, RDC 5.3 (0.35) and HOL 2.9, JER 3.8, RDC 4.9 (0.75), so 10 replicates could partly separate the loss from zero. To detect it (paired test, 5%, power 80%) would take about HOL 3, JER 5, RDC 12 replicates at weight 0.75 and HOL 115, JER 102, RDC 125 at 0.35. The positive NTM differences in some breeds cannot be distinguished from noise and are not evidence of a gain.
    • Simulation vs theory for NUE. NUE response relative to GS_NTM (simulated vs theory) was HOL 1.32 vs 1.32, JER 1.28 vs 1.36, RDC 1.25 vs 1.27 at 0.35 and HOL 1.42 vs 1.52, JER 1.28 vs 1.58, RDC 1.36 vs 1.43 at 0.75. The largest gap is 0.30. Where the simulated gain is smaller than theory, this is consistent with selection on EBVs: theory assumes true breeding values, while under GS_NTM the accuracy of the cows’ EBVs was 0.32 to 0.34 for NUE against 0.40 to 0.43 for protein yield, so part of the NUE weight is lost to prediction error (not tested directly). Which weight to use is a price decision for the breeding organisation. Because the simulated NTM cost is within noise, the price to use is the theoretical one in file 00 (EUR per cow-year per unit selection intensity). The EUR figures cover only the simulated part of NTM (see “What would change these conclusions”).
  3. MUN weight (GS_NTM_NUE35_MUN - GS_NTM_NUE35). Adding MUN at -0.35 on top of NUE 0.35 changed NUE by HOL +0.05 (p = 0.725), JER -0.22 (p = 0.371), RDC +0.05 (p = 0.664) and MUN by HOL -1.42 (p < 0.001), JER -1.34 (p < 0.001), RDC -1.24 (p < 0.001), at an NTM cost of HOL -49.8 (p = 0.037), JER -31.1 (p = 0.086), RDC -43.1 (p = 0.042) EUR per cow-year. Correa-Luna et al. (2021) found that low-MUN breeding values did not improve NUE, and the relation of MUN to urinary N is phenotypic, diet-driven and breed-specific (Mangwe et al. 2025; Burren et al. 2025), so a MUN weight is justified only if urinary N or ammonia gets its own value in the breeding goal.
  4. Methane weight (GS_NTM_NUE75_CH4 - GS_NTM_NUE75). The CH4 weight -0.5 is the knee of the sweep in file 00 (largest CH4 reduction per % NTM given up, selection-index theory). In the simulation it changed CH4 by HOL -1.58 (p < 0.001), JER -1.48 (p < 0.001), RDC -1.43 (p < 0.001), NUE by HOL -0.28 (p = 0.181), JER -0.16 (p = 0.349), RDC -0.16 (p = 0.134) and NTM value by HOL -39.4 (p < 0.001), JER -28.3 (p = 0.015), RDC -36.7 (p = 0.036) EUR per cow-year. Under NTM alone CH4 rose (HOL 1.89, JER 1.60, RDC 2.10). Real-world context: Nordic and Norwegian evaluations of methane are being developed from sniffer and GreenFeed data (Heringstad et al., ICAR 2026; Nielsen et al., ICAR 2026); the CH4 trait here is a concentration-type trait with the correlations of file 00, so the size of the response depends on those parameters.
  5. One joint evaluation across Denmark, Sweden, Finland and Germany, unless a GxE test on real data shows a between-country rg credibly below 0.80. In this simulation GxE of rg = 0.9 could not be estimated precisely from the subsample (see the GxE section).
  6. Optimum contribution selection with ΔF = 1% per generation, then mate allocation. Unconstrained genomic selection on the NTM + NUE 0.35 index raised inbreeding by 1.8% to 2.2% per generation; OCS at 1% brought this to 0.7% to 1.0%. The cost was NUE HOL -0.13 (p = 0.414), JER -0.70 (p = 0.003), RDC -0.18 (p = 0.220) and NTM value HOL -38.4 (p = 0.042), JER -29.5 (p = 0.033), RDC -30.2 (p = 0.044) EUR per cow-year. Mate allocation alone (single run) lowered genomic F after 10 generations (HOL 0.10, RDC 0.16, JER 0.16 vs 0.17/0.24/0.26 without it) but its rate of inbreeding was still 0.8% to 1.2% per generation, above the 1% guideline (inbreeding section).
  7. Records needed, given the low h2 of NUE: CFIT feed intake for N intake, plus milk protein and MUN from routine recording. Predicted NUE (MIR-based, Chen et al. 2021; or from diet energy, diet CP, milk yield and milk protein, Padberg et al. 2026, CCC 0.78) is the realistic phenotype; measured urinary N is not available at scale. In the multi-trait model, accuracy of NUE EBVs of cows without NUE records was UN 0.09, DIAG 0.01, FA -0.04: modelling the genetic covariances helped only in the unstructured (UN) model.

11 What would change these conclusions

  • Genetic correlations: 40 of 55 trait pairs are sourced (rg_evidence.xlsx; most are proxies or from Norwegian Red, Polish or Dutch cattle rather than the simulated breeds); the rest carry values implied by weighted bending, not estimates. All four NUE correlations come from one grazing Irish study (Tavernier et al. 2024). With a lower PY–NUE correlation, as Chen et al. (2021) imply for confinement Holstein, the NUE index would gain more NUE over the production index.
  • The NTM part of the goal is partial: the simulated sub-indices carry HOL 64%, RDC 64%, JER 72% of the total NTM weight (May 2026). The non-simulated sub-indices (calving, health, conformation, growth, youngstock survival) would take selection pressure, so absolute responses and EUR values here are too large; fat yield is missing from Yield; Jersey uses the Holstein milk:protein ratio; Saved Feed enters with its own published parameters (ReFI h2, NAV Saved Feed index correlations), not computed from ECM, body-weight change and DMI, because no kg-scale variances were available for that formula (file 00).
  • Founder sampling: each replicate has its own founders, so this source of variation is included; the coalescent demography (Ne history, breed split times) is the same for all replicates.
  • A full-size run (all 25,614 cows genotyped) on a cluster, which would also allow GxE to be estimated.
